title: Romeo & Juliet at The Delacorte - Free Shakespeare In The Park presen...
transcript: Don't get me wrong, I love when a revival is a reinvention, but it does get to a point. This summer's first free Shakespeare production in Central Park is a Romeo and Juliet that's visually stunning but lacking in thematic integrity. The heavy usage of Spanish throughout the production and the giant wall spanning the entire stage indicate that this tale of star-crossed lovers is now a tale of border-crossed lovers. The vibrant costumes and other design elements are full of cultural references, and the general time and place of this production is solidly planted. But while the families are clearly politically divided, it's not so clear where they are actually sociopolitically positioned in this moment. It's explicitly stated that the Capulets and the Montagues are “both alike in dignity,” yet this production almost frames it as the oppressors versus the oppressed. Perhaps the vagueness is intentional so as to not overtly disturb what I would argue is the key element that makes the fate of Romeo and Juliet so tragic — the fact that both families are equally at fault. With how explicit some of the messaging is, though, it's as if the production is trying to have it both ways, and it just feels muddy. For all its misses in its direction, I was very impressed by the performances, especially the chemistry between the titular ill-fated lovers. The two of them, in their scenes alone, fill the massive stage just as easily as the entire cast in the grander sequences. Deirdre O'connell is another highlight, along with Caleb Eberhardt as the Nurse and Mercutio, respectively — There's humor sprinkled throughout the entire cast, but these two really carry it. While the pacing is a little slow at times, I won't fault this production for that — I've always found Romeo and Juliet to be slow despite the relatively breakneck speed of their rise and fall. I was still very much in it with them thanks to the great scene work and dynamic staging, and it's still a production worth seeing. Attending a show at the Delacorte is always a special experience. This show didn't fully land for me, but what better place to witness big swings than the open air of Central Park with 1800 New Yorkers equally eager to spend their time? With that, another program for my collection.
reasoning: Reviewer criticizes muddy thematic direction and vague sociopolitical framing but praises performances, chemistry, and staging. Ultimately calls it 'worth seeing' while acknowledging it didn't fully land — a mixed lean-positive verdict.
